title: Trump Fires FEC Chair Weintraub, Paralyzing Campaign Finance Enforcement
description_short: Trump Fires FEC Chair Weintraub, Paralyzing Campaign Finance Enforcement
description_medium: Trump attempted to remove Federal Election Commission chair Ellen Weintraub in January 2025, an action she disputed as unlawful. Reporting links her removal and other vacancies to the commission's subsequent loss of a four-member quorum. Without that quorum, the agency's ability to conduct enforcement, issue advisory opinions, and make rules was constrained, raising concerns about campaign-finance oversight.
description_long: On January 31, 2025, President Trump sent a letter to Federal Election Commission Commissioner and Chair Ellen Weintraub stating You are hereby removed as a Member of the Federal Election Commission, effective immediately. Weintraub, who had served since 2002 after appointment by George W. Bush, declared the firing illegal under the Federal Election Campaign Act. Combined with two prior vacancies — Republican Sean Cooksey's January resignation and Allen Dickerson's April 30, 2025 resignation — the FEC dropped to three commissioners, losing the four-member quorum required for enforcement actions, advisory opinions, and rulemaking. This was only the fourth quorum loss in FEC history. The agency charged with policing campaign finance laws was effectively paralyzed during a period when Trump allies were raising unprecedented political funds. Democrats sued to block Trump's executive order asserting White House control over independent agencies including the FEC.

He has to lead now. It has gone too far and gotten out of hand — implying he knew his father was watching and failing to respond. The texts established that Trump's own son recognized the violence was real and the president was deliberately failing to stop it.

existing.title: Election Certification Interference - Training Trump Supporters to Block Results
existing.description_short: Election Certification Interference - Training Trump Supporters to Block Results
existing.description_long: Donald Trump and his allies systematically trained supporters across battleground states to pressure local election officials into refusing to certify election results, creating a coordinated infrastructure to steal elections through procedural sabotage at the county level. Law professor David Clements, a prominent election fraud conspiracy theorist, organized events with thousands of attendees across more than 40 counties in over a dozen states, including critical battlegrounds like Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina, and Pennsylvania, teaching Trump supporters how to intimidate certification officials. The training sessions focused on exploiting the ministerial duty of certification by encouraging Trump supporters to claim fraud without evidence and demand that county commissioners refuse to certify results, potentially disenfranchising entire counties. State election officials responded by issuing stern warnings that certification is mandatory, with Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes stating that counties failing to certify 'risk facing indictment.' The interference campaign built on lessons from 2020, when some Trump-supporting election officials attempted to delay or refuse certification before ultimately being forced to comply with their legal duties. Federal and state courts had already ruled that certification is a ministerial function that election officials cannot refuse based on personal beliefs about fraud, but Trump's network continued training supporters to pressure officials into violating these legal requirements. The systematic training represents an unprecedented attempt to steal elections through coordinated local-level sabotage of the certification process.

The mass firing represented the most extensive politicization of the federal government in American history, as Trump sought to install loyalists throughout the executive branch regardless of qualifications or experience. The purge targeted not just political appointees but career employees in agencies like Justice, State, Defense, and Health and Human Services, eliminating institutional knowledge and expertise built over decades. Trump justified the mass firings by claiming these employees had 'weaponized' the government against him, despite most being nonpartisan professionals who had served Republican and Democratic administrations alike. The systematic removal of experienced civil servants created chaos throughout the federal government, as critical functions were left unstaffed or run by inexperienced political appointees. The purge extended to scientists, economists, lawyers, and other professionals whose expertise was deemed threatening to Trump's political agenda. In his March 14, 2025 speech to the Justice Department, Trump explicitly described the firings as part of his campaign for 'accountability' against those who had opposed him. The mass purge represented the completion of Trump's authoritarian capture of the federal government, transforming professional civil service into a loyalty-based patronage system where expertise was subordinated to political fealty.

The Secure Communities and TPS termination represented Project 2025's vision of immigration based on deportation rather than protection, eliminating humanitarian programs that had historically provided safety for vulnerable populations while forcing legal immigrants into deportable status regardless of community ties, family relationships, or cooperation with American law enforcement agencies.

title: Vance conflates fraud estimates with proven fraud in convention speech
description_short: Vance conflates fraud estimates with proven fraud in convention speech
description_medium: JD Vance portrayed approximately $250 billion on an administration fraud ledger as uncovered fraud and claimed job gains had shifted from unauthorized immigrants to citizens. description_long:
JD Vance used a convention speech to portray approximately $250 billion on an administration fraud ledger as fraud that had been uncovered. He also claimed that job gains had shifted from unauthorized immigrants to citizens. PolitiFact examined both statements as part of the same appearance.

For the fraud claim, PolitiFact distinguished an estimate of fraud from totals produced by enforcement. Treating an estimated amount as money newly uncovered changes what the figure demonstrates. For the employment claim, the fact check explained that the foreign-born category includes naturalized citizens and legal residents. It therefore cannot simply be equated with unauthorized immigrants.

These distinctions concern the meaning of the numbers and population categories Vance invoked. They do not establish that every statement in the speech was false or quantify an unprovided employment breakdown. Vance linked the two figures in his broader argument about the administration’s record on fraud and employment. The fact check identified limitations in both comparisons.
